To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

In a cohort of HIV-positive individuals, unstructured antiretrovial therapy interruptions (TIs), defined as a patient initiated gap in treatment ≥ 90 days during the study window, were significantly associated with younger age, current illicit drug use, <95 % treatment adherence in the first 12 months of treatment, living with another person, and poor perception of overall general health.

unstructured treatment interruptions were associated with illicit drug use, low adherence in the first 12 months of treatment, living on the street, being unemployed, younger age at interview, and poor perception of overall physical and mental health.

unstructured antiretrovial treatment interruptions are common in British Columbia and are associated with current illicit substance use, poor adherence, homelessness, unemployment, younger age, and poorer self-perceived overall health.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying the correlates of unstructured antiretrovial therapy interruption in a cohort of HIV-positive individuals in British Columbia.
the social determinants of health, which are known to have a significant impact on the health of individuals living with HIV.
the factors that influence the decision of HIV-positive individuals to discontinue their treatment.

TIs were associated with current illicit substance use, poor self-reported health, living in a crowded environment, and being unemployed.

the following factors were associated with unstructured antiretrovial treatment interruption in this cohort: current illicit drug use, <95% adherence in the 1st year of treatment, living with at least 1 person or living on the streets, poor perception of overall heath, being unemployed, and younger age at time of interview.
TIs are more common among those with poor adherence, poor health perception, illicit drug use and homelessness.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the following factors are associated with TIs: current illicit drug use, low treatment adherence, living in unstable housing situations, poor perception of overall physical health, unemployment and younger age.

TIs are more common in people living with HIV in British Columbia, Canada, who have a lower CD4 cell count at treatment initiation, who are younger, who use drugs or who have poor health, who are unemployed and who live in a shared or homeless environment.

there is a need to improve access to services, particularly for individuals living on the street, and that there is a critical need for interventions to support adherence among patients who are currently experiencing difficulties with adherence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
TIs in British Columbia are associated with a variety of socioeconomic and health-related factors.
there are a significant number of people with HIV who have experienced a TI and that there are several correlates of TIs that can be used to inform interventions to support treatment retention.

TIs are associated with several factors, including illicit drug use, unemployment and living on the streets, and are not limited to patients with low CD4 cell counts, low adherence or poor perceptions of their own health.
